title: Learning to Solve Generative ODEs Beyond the Linear Span

paper.title: Learning to Solve Generative ODEs Beyond the Linear Span
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion and flow generative models sample by integrating a learned ODE, but high quality still requires many sequential model evaluations.
Solver learning reduces this cost by adapting scalar coefficients, timesteps, or both, while keeping the backbone model fixed.
In this work, we identify a structural bottleneck in this update family: each step remains span-limited.
Since the scalar-coefficient update lies in the span of buffered velocity evaluations, it can fit only the in-span component while leaving any out-of-span residual unreachable by scalar recombination alone.
We propose SpanLift, a lightweight neural solver that augments scalar-coefficient updates with a spatial residual operator.
SpanLift keeps a fixed base solver as an in-span prior and learns a spatial residual operator over the state and velocity buffer.
The operator is trained by endpoint teacher matching, preserves the pretrained backbone, and adds no model NFEs.
Empirically, the learned correction transfers across base solvers and is predominantly out-of-span.
Across pixel-space diffusion, latent flow matching, and precipitation nowcasting, SpanLift achieves state-of-the-art few-step sampling.
With only 3 NFE, it improves CIFAR-10 FID from 8.16 to 5.69 and ImageNet FID from 17.37 to 11.83.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Diffusion and flow generative models have become a powerful backbone for high-quality synthesis, leading to extensive use in content generation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] as well as scientific applications, from protein design [ 6 , 7 ] to weather forecasting [ 8 ] . Despite the high quality of outputs from these models, inference remains costly because generating each example requires many evaluations of the learned score/velocity model along the generative ODE. To close this gap, model distillation methods [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] train a student model to approximate multi-step sampling with fewer evaluations. However, they require substantial training cost and may alter the behavior of the original model. Another alternative is to keep the model frozen and improve the numerical solver. Analytic multistep solvers [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] improve sampling efficiency by combining current and buffered model outputs without extra model evaluations, which can be viewed as quadratures over the learned velocity field [ 16 , 17 ] . Here, analytically derived coefficients rely on small-step assumptions. In the low NFE regime, this premise breaks down, since large steps render low-degree local approximations unreliable [ 18 ] , and fixed coefficients cannot adapt to the nonstationary nature of the sampling dynamics [ 19 ] . The limitations of analytic solvers have motivated “solver learning”, which learns the sampling rule for integrating the generative ODE with only a few model evaluations. These methods usually follow a teacher-student setup, where a high-accuracy teacher sampler provides reference outputs and a lower NFE student solver is trained to reproduce them, either through trajectory-level or rollout-level supervision. Within this framework, existing work mainly adapts two solver choices. One cluster of works learns step-dependent coefficients for combining current and buffered model outputs, replacing analytically derived quadrature weights [ 20 , 18 , 19 ] . Another set of results learn where to query the model along the trajectory, by optimizing timestep schedules or intermediate evaluation points [ 21 , 22 ] . Such work [ 18 , 19 , 23 ] exists to learn both. This lets the solver adapt to large step sampling, where analytic quadrature becomes unreliable. Observation. This raises a natural question: under an extreme NFE budget, can better scalar combinations or quadrature points alone close the gap to the teacher? Despite differing in what they learn, existing methods still execute each step by scalar-recombining the available velocity evaluations, confining the update to the velocity-buffer span. We observe through a controlled ODE analysis (Figure 3 ) that such local confinement leaves a systematic gap. Decomposing the update mismatch into an in-span component and an orthogonal out-of-span residual, we find that scalar-coefficient learning can reduce the former by moving toward the best in-span projection, but cannot reduce the latter with any scalar recombination. Few-step sampling is therefore not only a matter of optimizing scalar coefficients or evaluation points. Once the velocity history at a step is fixed, further reducing the out-of-span residual calls for enlarging the class of admissible solver updates beyond the velocity-buffer span. This paper. We propose SpanLift , a solver framework that augments scalar-coefficient updates with a lightweight spatial operator. The base solver preserves the reliability of existing multistep samplers, while the learned operator supplies residual corrections beyond the history span, using neighboring states and model outputs to capture spatially coupled directions suggested by the local structure of generative ODEs. SpanLift uses endpoint teacher matching with the generative model frozen, adding no model evaluations beyond lightweight residual operator overhead . Across image generation with pixel-space diffusion and latent flow-matching models, as well as precipitation nowcasting, our solver achieves state-of-the-art few-step results with large margins, with larger gains under more extreme NFE budgets. In addition, SpanLift consistently improves diverse base solvers, from Runge–Kutta to scalar-coefficient multistep solvers, indicating the learned operator captures correction structure not tied to a particular update rule. These results show that treating the sampler itself as a lightweight neural solver provides a general and efficient route to stronger few-step sampling. sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: We consider deterministic sampling from a pretrained diffusion or flow-matching model in continuous time, starting from a noise sample at t = 0 t=0 and evolving toward the clean sample at t = 1 t=1 . Sampling follows the ODE x ˙ ​ ( t ) = u t ​ ( x ⁡ ( t ) ) \dot{x}(t)=u_{t}(x(t)) , t ∈ [ 0 , 1 ] t\in[0,1] , with initial condition x ⁡ ( 0 ) = x 0 ∼ p 0 x(0)=x_{0}\sim p_{0} , where u t ​ ( x ) = μ t ​ x + γ t ​ f θ ​ ( x , t ) u_{t}(x)\;=\;\mu_{t}\,x\;+\;\gamma_{t}\,f_{\theta}(x,t) (1) is the time-dependent velocity field induced by the frozen pretrained network f θ f_{\theta} . The scalar functions μ t , γ t \mu_{t},\gamma_{t} are determined by the noise schedule, e.g. , for flow-matching models, μ t = 0 \mu_{t}=0 and γ t = 1 \gamma_{t}=1 . The sampling objective is to numerically integrate this ODE and obtain the clean sample x ⁡ ( 1 ) x(1) . For any two times t i < t i + 1 t_{i}<t_{i+1} , the exact solution satisfies x ⁡ ( t i + 1 ) = x ⁡ ( t i ) + ∫ t i t i + 1 u t ​ ( x ⁡ ( t ) ) ​ 𝑑 t x(t_{i+1})=x(t_{i})+\int_{t_{i}}^{t_{i+1}}u_{t}(x(t))\,dt . In practice, we introduce a time discretization 0 = t 0 < t 1 < ⋯ < t N = 1 0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{N}=1 and compute an approximate trajectory x i ≈ x ⁡ ( t i ) x_{i}\approx x(t_{i}) by replacing the integral with a computable approximation. A generic solver step takes the increment form x i + 1 = x i + h i ​ Δ i , h i := t i + 1 − t i , x_{i+1}=x_{i}+h_{i}\,\Delta_{i},\qquad h_{i}:=t_{i+1}-t_{i}, (2) where Δ i \Delta_{i} denotes the solver update at step i i . Standard solvers include Euler, Heun, and higher-order Runge–Kutta (RK) methods. Higher-order RK variants reduce local discretization error via additional evaluations, but in the few-step regime, we find that these quickly consume the limited NFE budget.

sections.heading: 2.1 Multistep solvers for few-step sampling
sections.text: Rather than spending additional network evaluations at each step, modern few-step samplers [ 24 , 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 , 25 ] reuse a buffer of previously computed model outputs to construct each update. In their multistep form, the update direction is a linear combination of buffered velocity evaluations. Let u i := u t i ​ ( x i ) u_{i}:=u_{t_{i}}(x_{i}) denote the model velocity at the current numerical state. A K K -step multistep update is written as Δ i = ∑ j = 0 K − 1 w i , j ana ​ u i − j , \Delta_{i}\;=\;\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}w_{i,j}^{\rm ana}\,u_{i-j}, (3) where { u i − j } j = 0 K − 1 \{u_{i-j}\}_{j=0}^{K-1} are the buffered velocity fields from the current and past K − 1 K{-}1 steps. For example, iPNDM [ 14 ] can be viewed as an extrapolatory polynomial quadrature rule over the velocity buffer, where its coefficients reduce to the classical Adams–Bashforth weights under uniform discretization, forming the increment by extrapolating from three historical velocity fields. The multistep variant of DPM-Solver++ [ 12 ] also takes the form ( 3 ), with step-dependent coefficients derived from the semi-linear structure of the diffusion ODE in logSNR parameterization. In these handcrafted solvers, w i , j w_{i,j} are derived analytically from the chosen solver family and time discretization.

sections.heading: 2.2 Learnable multistep solvers for few-step sampling
sections.text: Recently, learnable approaches [ 26 , 20 , 27 , 18 , 28 , 19 , 21 , 29 , 30 , 31 , 22 , 32 , 33 , 34 ] have been proposed in place of fully handcrafted solvers. These methods aim to improve few-step sampling by learning better solver design choices, either by learning the better combination of buffered velocities, or by learning better quadrature points , i.e. , a better timestep schedule, or both.

sections.heading: Learning solver parameters.
sections.text: These methods commonly use a teacher-student framework, where a high-accuracy teacher solver produces reference samples and a lower-NFE student solver is trained to reproduce them. The methods differ in where the teacher supervision is applied. One line of work [ 22 , 32 , 23 , 35 , 26 ] provides trajectory-level supervision, training the student to match the teacher at each coarse-grid time t i t_{i} . However, recent results [ 21 , 18 , 19 ] show that it can be overly restrictive in the low-NFE regime. With large step sizes, the student may achieve a better final output by deviating from the teacher trajectory at intermediate times. Thus, an alternative approach [ 20 , 21 , 18 , 19 , 34 ] supervises only the final rollout endpoint . Given a student solver S S induces a rollout map Φ S : x 0 ↦ x ^ 1 S \Phi_{S}:x_{0}\mapsto\hat{x}_{1}^{S} by recursively applying its update rule over N N steps, and a teacher rollout map Φ ⋆ \Phi^{\star} with a finer discretization, the student is trained to match the teacher’s final output: S N † = arg ⁡ min S ∈ 𝒮 N ⁡ 𝒥 ⁡ ( S ) , 𝒥 ⁡ ( S ) := 𝔼 x 0 ∼ p 0 ​ [ ℓ ⁡ ( Φ S ​ ( x 0 ) , Φ ⋆ ​ ( x 0 ) ) ] , S_{N}^{\dagger}=\arg\hskip-4.0pt\min_{S\in\mathcal{S}_{N}}\mathcal{J}(S),\qquad\mathcal{J}(S):=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0}\sim p_{0}}\bigl[\ell\bigl(\Phi_{S}(x_{0}),\,\Phi^{\star}(x_{0})\bigr)\bigr], (4) where ℓ \ell is the distance between the student and teacher outputs. Note that endpoint supervision is applied only after the recursive rollout, thus does not define a unique target update at each coarse step. Different per-step update sequences can reach the same endpoint without corresponding to teacher-trajectory velocities.

sections.heading: What is learned?
sections.text: Existing methods optimize one or both of two solver components. The first is the combination of buffered velocities. Methods such as DLMS [ 35 ] , S4S [ 18 ] , and DyWeight [ 19 ] learn step-dependent scalar coefficients W := [ w i , j ] ∈ ℝ N × K W:=[w_{i,j}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times K} , Δ i ​ ( W ) = ∑ j = 0 K − 1 w i , j learn ​ u i − j . \Delta_{i}(W)=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}w_{i,j}^{\rm learn}\,u_{i-j}. (5) The second is the timestep schedule, i.e. , the quadrature points at which the solver is executed, as in GITS [ 36 ] , AYS [ 31 ] , and LD3 [ 21 ] . More recent methods optimize both jointly, e.g. , S4S-Alt [ 18 ] alternates between coefficient and schedule learning, while DyWeight [ 19 ] parameterizes both the velocity combination and effective step size through a shared weight table. Despite these differences, all proposals above still execute each step as a scalar-weighted combination of the velocity evaluations available at that step .

sections.heading: 3.1 Linear span limitation
sections.text: Scalar-coefficient solvers can improve the choice of weights over the velocity history, but their updates remain confined to the span induced by that history. We analyze this restriction by decomposing a reference update into its in-span component and the remaining out-of-span residual.

Every scalar-coefficient update satisfies Δ i ∈ 𝒱 i \Delta_{i}\in\mathcal{V}_{i} , regardless of whether the coefficients are fixed analytically or learned from data. We write Π 𝒱 i \Pi_{\mathcal{V}_{i}} for the orthogonal projection onto 𝒱 i \mathcal{V}_{i} .

sections.heading: 3.2 From scalar coefficients to learned operators
sections.text: Next, we enlarge the scalar-coefficient update family by viewing solver steps as operators over the velocity buffer. This operator view includes scalar combinations, pointwise maps, and spatial operators as increasingly expressive update classes, providing a compact design space beyond 𝒱 i \mathcal{V}_{i} and motivating spatial kernels as a lightweight inductive bias for residuals with cross-position structure.

sections.heading: Operator view of solver updates.
sections.text: We view each solver step as an operator over the available velocity buffer X i := ( u i , u i − 1 , … , u i − K + 1 ) . X_{i}:=(u_{i},u_{i-1},\ldots,u_{i-K+1}). The scalar-coefficient update is recovered as 𝒜 i scalar ​ ( X i ) = ∑ j = 0 K − 1 w i , j ​ u i − j , [ 𝒜 i scalar ​ ( X i ) ] p = ∑ j = 0 K − 1 w i , j ​ I C ​ u i − j ​ [ p ] , \mathcal{A}_{i}^{\rm scalar}(X_{i})=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}w_{i,j}u_{i-j},\qquad[\mathcal{A}_{i}^{\rm scalar}(X_{i})]_{p}=\sum_{j=0}^{K-1}w_{i,j}I_{C}\,u_{i-j}[p], (9) where I C I_{C} is the channel-wise identity matrix. sections.heading: 4 SpanLift: An operator-augmented neural solver
sections.text: The previous section motivates enlarging scalar-coefficient solvers with an operator that can access directions outside the velocity-buffer span. We instantiate the operator view above as SpanLift , an operator-augmented neural solver built on top of a strong scalar-coefficient base solver. The base solver provides a reliable in-span update, while the learned operator supplies additional directions beyond the velocity-buffer span.

sections.heading: Residual operator parameterization.
sections.text: Let X i = ( u i , u i − 1 , … , u i − K + 1 ) X_{i}=(u_{i},u_{i-1},\ldots,u_{i-K+1}) denote the velocity buffer from Section 3.2 . We write the base update as Δ i base = 𝒜 i base ​ ( X i ) , \Delta_{i}^{\rm base}=\mathcal{A}_{i}^{\rm base}(X_{i}), where 𝒜 i base \mathcal{A}_{i}^{\rm base} is an analytic or learned scalar-coefficient solver, such as ( 9 ). SpanLift augments this update with a learned residual operator: Δ i SL = α i ​ Δ i base + β i ​ Δ i op , Δ i op = ℛ ϕ ​ ( X ~ i , ξ i ) , \Delta_{i}^{\rm SL}=\alpha_{i}\,\Delta_{i}^{\rm base}+\beta_{i}\,\Delta_{i}^{\rm op},\qquad\Delta_{i}^{\rm op}=\mathcal{R}_{\phi}(\widetilde{X}_{i};\xi_{i}), (14) where α i \alpha_{i} and β i \beta_{i} are step-wise learnable scalars, ℛ ϕ \mathcal{R}_{\phi} is a learned spatial residual operator, and X ~ i := Concat ⁡ ( x i , u i , u i − 1 , … , u i − K + 1 ) \widetilde{X}_{i}:=\operatorname{Concat}(x_{i},u_{i},u_{i-1},\ldots,u_{i-K+1}) is the residual-operator input. The conditioning variable ξ i = [ t i , λ i , h i ] \xi_{i}=[t_{i},\lambda_{i},h_{i}] provides the current time, logSNR, and step size. We initialize the residual branch close to the base solver, e.g. , with α i = 1 \alpha_{i}=1 and β i \beta_{i} set to zero or a small value. This parameterization separates the role of the base solver and the learned residual operator. The base update provides a strong in-span direction inherited from existing multistep solvers. The residual operator is not constrained to lie in 𝒱 i \mathcal{V}_{i} , and its spatial support enables the local q → p q\to p interactions in ( 11 ). We do not enforce Δ i op ⟂ 𝒱 i \Delta_{i}^{\rm op}\perp\mathcal{V}_{i} , nor do we supervise it with the local residual r i ⟂ r_{i}^{\perp} . Instead, the endpoint objective determines how the operator uses its extra degrees of freedom across the rollout. The base solver acts as a solver prior, so the learned operator only needs to model the remaining endpoint error while retaining the inductive bias of existing multistep solvers. At each step, we evaluate the frozen generative model once to obtain u i u_{i} , form Δ i base \Delta_{i}^{\rm base} from the velocity buffer, compute Δ i op \Delta_{i}^{\rm op} using ℛ ϕ \mathcal{R}_{\phi} , and update x i + 1 = x i + h i ​ ( α i ​ Δ i base + β i ​ Δ i op ) . x_{i+1}=x_{i}+h_{i}\bigl(\alpha_{i}\Delta_{i}^{\rm base}+\beta_{i}\Delta_{i}^{\rm op}\bigr). (15) Since ℛ ϕ \mathcal{R}_{\phi} does not call the pretrained velocity model, the method does not increase model NFE; it only adds a lightweight neural overhead.

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: We instantiate ℛ ϕ \mathcal{R}_{\phi} as a shallow FiLM-conditioned CNN. A 1 × 1 1{\times}1 stem first mixes the channel dimension of X ~ i \widetilde{X}_{i} . Then, FiLM-modulated residual blocks with depthwise spatial convolutions provide the spatial mixing motivated in Section 3.2 . A final convolutional head maps the features to the residual update Δ i op \Delta_{i}^{\rm op} . The default configuration uses hidden dimension d = 64 d=64 with two residual blocks, yielding negligible parameter overhead relative to the frozen diffusion or flow model. Full architectural details are provided in Appendix A.

sections.heading: Training objective.
sections.text: We train SpanLift end-to-end through the full N N -step rollout using the teacher-matching objective 𝒥 \mathcal{J} in ( 4 ). Thus, gradients reflect the cumulative effect of each residual update on the final output, rather than supervising each step with a fixed local target. Following prior learned-solver methods [ 21 , 18 , 19 ] , we choose the per-sample loss ℓ \ell according to the model type. For pixel-space diffusion models [ 2 ] , we use an Inception loss [ 38 ] . For latent flow-matching models [ 3 , 4 , 8 ] , the increased capacity of the spatial residual operator makes loss design more important. Because scalar solvers have limited capacity, they are less prone to fitting fine-grained latent ℓ 2 \ell_{2} discrepancies. A higher-capacity operator can match these details more directly, which may reduce latent MSE while degrading perceptual sharpness. We therefore supplement latent matching with an image-space perceptual term. Specifically, let z 1 ⋆ z_{1}^{\star} and z ^ 1 ϕ \hat{z}_{1}^{\phi} denote the final latents from teacher and SpanLift, and let D D denote the frozen decoder used only to compute image-space perceptual features. We use ℓ ⁡ ( z ^ 1 ϕ , z 1 ⋆ ) = c ​ ‖ z ^ 1 ϕ − z 1 ⋆ ‖ 2 + ‖ f DINO ​ ( D ⁡ ( z ^ 1 ϕ ) ) − f DINO ​ ( D ⁡ ( z 1 ⋆ ) ) ‖ 2 , \ell(\hat{z}_{1}^{\phi},z_{1}^{\star})=c\,\|\hat{z}_{1}^{\phi}-z_{1}^{\star}\|^{2}+\bigl\|f_{\rm DINO}(D(\hat{z}_{1}^{\phi}))-f_{\rm DINO}(D(z_{1}^{\star}))\bigr\|^{2}, (16) where f DINO f_{\rm DINO} denotes a frozen DINOv2 [ 39 ] and c = 0.1 c=0.1 . sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: We evaluate SpanLift in diverse few-step sampling settings, covering image generation with pixel-space diffusion and latent flow-matching models, and precipitation nowcasting. Our experiments address three questions: Q1. Does SpanLift improve few-step sampling across models/domains? Q2. Can SpanLift serve as a general residual operator across base solvers? Q3. Does the learned correction behave as the intended span-lifting residual? Regarding implementation details and more results, see the appendix.

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: For pixel-space generation, we use the official EDM [ 2 ] checkpoints on CIFAR-10 [ 41 ] , ImageNet [ 42 ] , FFHQ [ 43 ] , and AFHQv2 [ 44 ] . For latent flow matching, we evaluate SANA-0.6B [ 4 ] at 512 × 512 512{\times}512 resolution, with additional FLUX.1-dev [ 3 ] results in the appendix. SpanLift trains only the lightweight residual operator R ϕ R_{\phi} , while keeping the generative backbone and the base solver frozen. For pixel-space experiments, we follow the DyWeight [ 19 ] protocol, including the teacher solver and training set size, and report FID [ 40 ] over 50K generated samples. For SANA, we split MJHQ-30K into 5K training and 25K evaluation prompts. SpanLift and DyWeight are trained on the same precomputed teacher trajectories using 20-NFE iPNDM(2M), CFG = 4.5 =4.5 , and PAG disabled. We report FID and ImageReward [ 47 ] on the 25K evaluation set. Full hyperparameters and architectural details are provided in the appendix.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Tables 2 and 4 summarize the quantitative results. SpanLift achieves the lowest FID across all pixel space benchmarks and on SANA-0.6B, with larger gains at lower NFE. This pattern is consistent with our span perspective, where large steps can expose residual directions that are not well captured by scalar recombination, while the spatial residual operator can partially compensate for them. Figure 2 shows the qualitative results, where both analytic and learned scalar solvers fail to form recognizable scene structure, whereas SpanLift recovers coherent objects and layouts. Qualitative results on FLUX.1-dev further show improvements in local prompt details, including legible text on a cake topper and a correctly depicted hand-held phone (Figure 1 ). sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced SpanLift, a lightweight operator-augmented neural solver that lifts scalar-coefficient updates beyond the velocity-buffer span. SpanLift keeps the backbone fixed and preserves the model NFE budget while expanding the solver update family. Empirical analyses show that the learned correction transfers across base solvers and supplies predominantly out-of-span directions. Across all evaluated settings, SpanLift achieves state-of-the-art performance under the extreme NFE budgets.

Kim Affiliation: KAIST Abstract Diffusion and flow generative models sample by integrating a learned ODE, but high quality still requires many sequential model evaluations. Solver learning reduces this cost by adapting scalar coefficients, timesteps, or both, while keeping the backbone model fixed. In this work, we identify a structural bottleneck in this update family: each step remains span-limited. Since the scalar-coefficient update lies in the span of buffered velocity evaluations, it can fit only the in-span component while leaving any out-of-span residual unreachable by scalar recombination alone. We propose SpanLift, a lightweight neural solver that augments scalar-coefficient updates with a spatial residual operator. SpanLift keeps a fixed base solver as an in-span prior and learns a spatial residual operator over the state and velocity buffer. The operator is trained by endpoint teacher matching, preserves the pretrained backbone, and adds no model NFEs. Empirically, the learned correction transfers across base solvers and is predominantly out-of-span. Across pixel-space diffusion, latent flow matching, and precipitation nowcasting, SpanLift achieves state-of-the-art few-step sampling. With only 3 NFE, it improves CIFAR-10 FID from 8.16 to 5.69 and ImageNet FID from 17.37 to 11.83. § § footnotetext: Equal advising. 1 Introduction Diffusion and flow generative models have become a powerful backbone for high-quality synthesis, leading to extensive use in content generation [ 1 , 2 , 3 , 4 , 5 ] as well as scientific applications, from protein design [ 6 , 7 ] to weather forecasting [ 8 ] . Despite the high quality of outputs from these models, inference remains costly because generating each example requires many evaluations of the learned score/velocity model along the generative ODE. To close this gap, model distillation methods [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] train a student model to approximate multi-step sampling with fewer evaluations. However, they require substantial training cost and may alter the behavior of the original model. Another alternative is to keep the model frozen and improve the numerical solver. Analytic multistep solvers [ 12 , 13 , 14 , 15 ] improve sampling efficiency by combining current and buffered model outputs without extra model evaluations, which can be viewed as quadratures over the learned velocity field [ 16 , 17 ] . Here, analytically derived coefficients rely on small-step assumptions. In the low NFE regime, this premise breaks down, since large steps render low-degree local approximations unreliable [ 18 ] , and fixed coefficients cannot adapt to the nonstationary nature of the sampling dynamics [ 19 ] . The limitations of analytic solvers have motivated “solver learning”, which learns the sampling rule for integrating the generative ODE with only a few model evaluations. These methods usually follow a teacher-student setup, where a high-accuracy teacher sampler provides reference outputs and a lower NFE student solver is trained to reproduce them, either through trajectory-level or rollout-level supervision. Within this framework, existing work mainly adapts two solver choices. One cluster of works learns step-dependent coefficients for combining current and buffered model outputs, replacing analytically derived quadrature weights [ 20 , 18 , 19 ] . Another set of results learn where to query the model along the trajectory, by optimizing timestep schedules or intermediate evaluation points [ 21 , 22 ] . Such work [ 18 , 19 , 23 ] exists to learn both. This lets the solver adapt to large step sampling, where analytic quadrature becomes unreliable. Observation. This raises a natural question: under an extreme NFE budget, can better scalar combinations or quadrature points alone close the gap to the teacher? Despite differing in what they learn, existing methods still execute each step by scalar-recombining the available velocity evaluations, confining the update to the velocity-buffer span. We observe through a controlled ODE analysis (Figure 3 ) that such local confinement leaves a systematic gap. Decomposing the update mismatch into an in-span component and an orthogonal out-of-span residual, we find that scalar-coefficient learning can reduce the former by moving toward the best in-span projection, but cannot reduce the latter with any scalar recombination. Few-step sampling is therefore not only a matter of optimizing scalar coefficients or evaluation points. Once the velocity history at a step is fixed, further reducing the out-of-span residual calls for enlarging the class of admissible solver updates beyond the velocity-buffer span. This paper. We propose SpanLift , a solver framework that augments scalar-coefficient updates with a lightweight spatial operator. The base solver preserves the reliability of existing multistep samplers, while the learned operator supplies residual corrections beyond the history span, using neighboring states and model outputs to capture spatially coupled directions suggested by the local structure of generative ODEs. SpanLift uses endpoint teacher matching with the generative model frozen, adding no model evaluations beyond lightweight residual operator overhead . Across image generation with pixel-space diffusion and latent flow-matching models, as well as precipitation nowcasting, our solver achieves state-of-the-art few-step results with large margins, with larger gains under more extreme NFE budgets. In addition, SpanLift consistently improves diverse base solvers, from Runge–Kutta to scalar-coefficient multistep solvers, indicating the learned operator captures correction structure not tied to a particular update rule. These results show that treating the sampler itself as a lightweight neural solver provides a general and efficient route to stronger few-step sampling. Report HSS, LPIPS, CSI on SEVIR [ 46 ] . 5 Experiments We evaluate SpanLift in diverse few-step sampling settings, covering image generation with pixel-space diffusion and latent flow-matching models, and precipitation nowcasting. Our experiments address three questions: Q1. Does SpanLift improve few-step sampling across models/domains? Q2. Can SpanLift serve as a general residual operator across base solvers? Q3. Does the learned correction behave as the intended span-lifting residual? Regarding implementation details and more results, see the appendix. 5.1 Few-step image generation Experimental setup. For pixel-space generation, we use the official EDM [ 2 ] checkpoints on CIFAR-10 [ 41 ] , ImageNet [ 42 ] , FFHQ [ 43 ] , and AFHQv2 [ 44 ] . For latent flow matching, we evaluate SANA-0.6B [ 4 ] at 512 × 512 512{\times}512 resolution, with additional FLUX.1-dev [ 3 ] results in the appendix. SpanLift trains only the lightweight residual operator R ϕ R_{\phi} , while keeping the generative backbone and the base solver frozen. For pixel-space experiments, we follow the DyWeight [ 19 ] protocol, including the teacher solver and training set size, and report FID [ 40 ] over 50K generated samples. For SANA, we split MJHQ-30K into 5K training and 25K evaluation prompts. SpanLift and DyWeight are trained on the same precomputed teacher trajectories using 20-NFE iPNDM(2M), CFG = 4.5 =4.5 , and PAG disabled. We report FID and ImageReward [ 47 ] on the 25K evaluation set. Full hyperparameters and architectural details are provided in the appendix. Results. Tables 2 and 4 summarize the quantitative results. SpanLift achieves the lowest FID across all pixel space benchmarks and on SANA-0.6B, with larger gains at lower NFE. This pattern is consistent with our span perspective, where large steps can expose residual directions that are not well captured by scalar recombination, while the spatial residual operator can partially compensate for them. Figure 2 shows the qualitative results, where both analytic and learned scalar solvers fail to form recognizable scene structure, whereas SpanLift recovers coherent objects and layouts. SpanLift keeps the backbone fixed and preserves the model NFE budget while expanding the solver update family. Empirical analyses show that the learned correction transfers across base solvers and supplies predominantly out-of-span directions.
